title: Dynamic spanning trees with polylogarithmic average stretch
formal:
Is there a uniform randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains a spanning forest \(F_t\) of an unweighted simple graph \(G_t\) with polylogarithmic expected average stretch and sublinear expected amortized update time? Precisely, do there exist such an algorithm, constants \(C,a,c>0\), and a function \(u:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{u(n)}n=0,\]
such that for every \(n\ge2\) and every finite oblivious sequence of \(T\) edge insertions and deletions starting from the empty \(n\)-vertex graph,
\[\mathbb E[\operatorname{avstr}_{F_t}(G_t)]\le C(\log_2(n+2))^c\quad(0\le t\le T),\]
and the expected total work for the updates is at most \(T u(n)\), after at most \(C n^a\) expected initialization work? The maintained object must always be an actual spanning forest using current graph edges.

For a connected graph, a spanning forest is a spanning tree. The componentwise convention below makes the target meaningful when a deletion disconnects the graph, as in the original dynamic low-stretch algorithm. This card chooses the first question in the workshop source, with the expectation and amortization conventions of that prior work; it does not also require resistance to adaptive updates.
why: Low-stretch spanning trees replace a graph by a particularly simple subgraph while controlling average detours. They underpin graph optimization and linear-system algorithms. The question asks whether a polylogarithmic quality guarantee can survive repeated edge changes without spending a linear amount of work per update; it isolates the cost of requiring the approximation to remain a genuine subgraph.
status_note: The November 2022 Section 4.3, Forster–Goranci’s full author manuscript (Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2), and Forster–Goranci–Henzinger arXiv:2004.10319v2 introduction were read on 2026-09-14. The Chechik–Zhang 2020 bound is recorded through the checked workshop report rather than a claimed full reading of that paper. A bounded later-work search through this review date found no matching all-graph fully dynamic spanning-forest result with the selected quality and update bounds. Related probabilistic tree embeddings and dynamic spanners do not meet the subgraph-forest requirement. Status remains source-open with these limits.

progress.text: Forster and Goranci establish fully dynamic spanning forests with subpolynomial expected average stretch and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) expected amortized update time.
Chechik and Zhang improve the update time to \(n^{o(1)}\) while retaining subpolynomial stretch, as reported in the checked workshop source.
Dynamic probabilistic tree embeddings achieve additional quality/time tradeoffs for a different maintained object.
The workshop explicitly asks for polylogarithmic average stretch with sublinear fully dynamic updates.

sentences: A changing unweighted graph must retain a spanning tree in each connected component.
The quality measure is the average tree-path length between the endpoints of graph edges.
The question asks for polylogarithmic expected quality with sublinear expected amortized work per edge insertion or deletion.
The update sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s randomness, and disconnected intermediate graphs are covered.
Existing subpolynomial-stretch forests and polylogarithmic-stretch metric embeddings leave different parts of this target unresolved.

definitions:
The graph \(G_t=([n],E_t)\) is finite, undirected, loopless and simple, with unit edge lengths. Its vertex set remains fixed. An insertion specifies an absent edge between two distinct labels, and a deletion specifies a present edge. No maximum-degree or sparsity promise is imposed, and components may split or merge. A valid spanning forest \(F_t=([n],E_t^F)\) has \(E_t^F\subseteq E_t\), is acyclic, and connects every pair of vertices that lie in the same connected component of \(G_t\). Thus it contains one spanning tree for each nontrivial component and all isolated vertices.

For \(\{v,w\}\in E_t\), let \(d_{F_t}(v,w)\) be the number of edges on the unique path between its endpoints in \(F_t\). Put
\[\operatorname{avstr}_{F_t}(G_t)=\begin{cases}|E_t|^{-1}\displaystyle\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E_t}d_{F_t}(v,w),&|E_t|>0,\\0,&|E_t|=0.\end{cases}\]
All current edges participate in the average, including forest edges, whose distance is one. The target bounds this absolute stretch quantity, not its ratio to the best possible forest. The expectation is over the algorithm's internal randomness at each fixed time, after averaging over the graph edges; a bound for every individual edge is not required.

The update sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm's random choices and is revealed one operation at a time. The algorithm is not given future updates. Its guarantee covers every finite sequence length, and hence every finite prefix of any fixed infinite valid sequence. The same constants and function \(u\) work for all graphs, edge counts, times and sequences.

Use a word-RAM with \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit words for a fixed constant \(c_w\) large enough to address the algorithm's polynomially many persistent words. Unit-cost operations are word reads/writes, comparisons, branches, Boolean operations, shifts, modular addition/subtraction/multiplication, integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word, and independent uniform random words. The algorithm has one finite program for all \(n\); no input-dependent advice or uncharged precomputed table is allowed. Initialization starts with no graph edges and is charged separately as specified.

The forest is maintained explicitly as its edge set: a linked list or equivalent enumerable collection of its current edge records is stored, and each current graph edge record indicates whether it belongs to the forest. Given an existing edge-record handle, this flag is readable in constant time, and all forest edges can be enumerated in time proportional to their number plus one. Finding graph-edge records from endpoint labels, changing forest membership, random choices, rebuilds and memory management are included in update work. No full forest printout or rooted-parent array is required after every update.

Every completed update must produce a valid spanning forest, and each finite execution must terminate with probability one. Only the quality and runtime guarantees are in expectation. Amortized expected time bounds the sum of update costs; it imposes no worst-case per-update bound. The source's word 'sublinear' is made precise as \(o(n)\), without additionally requiring a fixed polynomial saving \(n^{1-\delta}\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence under the stated model. A positive result must simultaneously achieve the expected polylogarithmic average-stretch bound and an expected amortized update bound \(u(n)=o(n)\) on all valid fully dynamic graph sequences. A spanning forest with only \(n^{o(1)}\) stretch, a decremental-only algorithm, or a bound on an unrelated tree metric does not meet the target. The maintained forest must consist of graph edges; introducing auxiliary weighted tree edges or Steiner vertices is not allowed. A negative answer must apply to the stated randomized expected guarantees, not only to deterministic or worst-case variants.

context_blocks.text: The workshop source records static spanning trees of average stretch \(O(\log n\log\log n)\), and dynamic algorithms with subpolynomial stretch and update time. Its first open question asks to improve the stretch guarantee to a polylogarithm while keeping updates sublinear.

Forster and Goranci formulate the dynamic object as a spanning forest and analyze expected average stretch against an oblivious adversary. Their Corollary 1.2 gives \(n^{o(1)}\) expected average stretch and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) expected amortized update time.
The workshop reports Chechik–Zhang’s SODA 2020 improvement to \(n^{o(1)}\) expected amortized update time while retaining subpolynomial average stretch.

A subpolynomial function grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of its argument, but need not be bounded by a fixed power of its logarithm. Consequently, the recorded subpolynomial-stretch algorithms do not automatically meet the polylogarithmic quality target.

Forster, Goranci and Henzinger obtain dynamic probabilistic metric-tree embeddings with polylogarithmic expected stretch at suitable update-time tradeoffs. Such an embedding may use a tree that is not a subgraph of the changing graph. Their introduction explicitly distinguishes this result from maintaining low-average-stretch spanning trees.

The source separately asks for algorithms tolerating adaptive adversaries. That requirement is not combined with the first question here: the requested improvement already concerns sequences chosen independently of the random choices.
